sources.title: Trump Again Calls for CBS to Lose Its License, “60 Minutes” to Be Terminated
sources.access_notes: Source supplied in the packet; it covers Trump’s CBS-license comments, not simultaneous threats against the three networks named in the original.

sources.title: Why CBS stands at the epicenter of Trump’s assault on the media
sources.access_notes: NPR article opened. It explains the CBS dispute and notes the FCC’s authority derives from local broadcast stations’ licenses.

supported_facts: The evidence cited in the packet concerns Trump’s February 2025 threat against CBS over 60 Minutes and CBS’s local station licenses.
NPR explains that broadcast licenses are held by local stations rather than a single national network license.
unsupported_original_claims: No source reviewed verifies that Trump threatened to revoke licenses of MSNBC, ABC, and CBS together on Feb. 15 or repeatedly across early 2025.
Claims that network executives reported internal pressure to moderate coverage and that press-freedom indices downgraded the United States because of this episode are unsupported here.

corrected_claim.title: Trump Calls for CBS to Lose Its Broadcast Licenses During 60 Minutes Dispute
corrected_claim.claim: In early February 2025, Trump called for CBS to lose its broadcast licenses amid his dispute with 60 Minutes. FCC licenses attach to local broadcast stations, so the episode should not be described as revoking a single license held by each national network.

access_notes: NPR page directly opened; TVNewsCheck report is the specific event source included with the packet.
evidence_gap: A separate source is needed for any distinct threats against ABC or MSNBC, network-level internal pressure, or measured press-freedom consequences.

sources.title: Final Report of the Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol, Appendix 3
sources.publisher: U.S. House Select Committee report (text transcription hosted by Wikisource)
sources.access_notes: Appendix text opened. It says Trump and the RNC raised more than $250 million after the election and that much was not used to stop the purported steal.

supported_facts: The January 6 Committee report says Trump and the RNC raised more than $250 million after the 2020 election using Stop the Steal messaging.
The report says most post-election fundraising was diverted from the stated election-defense purpose.
unsupported_original_claims: The report does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. personally led the fundraising operation.
The entry’s claims about his rallies, emails, and posts as the cause of anger culminating in Jan. 6 are not demonstrated by this appendix.

corrected_claim.title: Trump Campaign and RNC Raised More Than $250 Million After the 2020 Election
corrected_claim.claim: The January 6 Committee reported that Trump and the RNC raised more than $250 million after the 2020 election using false fraud claims and Stop the Steal fundraising messages; much of the money was diverted from election-defense purposes.

access_notes: The committee report text is readable at the linked transcription. The entry’s personal attribution to Trump Jr. is not carried forward.
evidence_gap: A source naming Trump Jr. as the operation’s leader and documenting his specific fundraising role is needed before attributing the campaign to him personally.

sources.title: Trump’s Castle and Plaza file for bankruptcy
sources.access_notes: Contemporaneous UPI report opened. It says Trump Castle and Trump Plaza filed prepackaged Chapter 11 plans and reports their bondholders’ approval.

supported_facts: Trump Castle and Trump Plaza filed prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy plans in March 1992.
UPI reported the Castle’s cash-flow difficulties and the restructuring’s debt-for-equity terms.
unsupported_original_claims: The record’s Sept. 1, 1992 date is wrong; UPI dates the report and filing to March 9, 1992.
This article does not substantiate the claims about vendor losses, junk-bond financing as the cause, or regulators allowing Trump to retain a management role.

corrected_claim.title: Trump Castle and Trump Plaza File Prepackaged Chapter 11 Plans in March 1992
corrected_claim.claim: Contemporaneous UPI reporting on March 9, 1992 said Trump Castle and Trump Plaza filed prepackaged Chapter 11 plans after bondholders approved restructuring terms.

access_notes: UPI archive report directly opened and read.
evidence_gap: Claims about creditor losses, financing structure, and Trump’s retained management role require separate bankruptcy-court records or contemporaneous reporting.

sources.title: US Department of Homeland Security firing all advisory committee members, letter says
sources.access_notes: Reuters story carried by Investing.com opened. It identifies a Jan. 20 letter signed by Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman and describes DHS advisory committees.

supported_facts: A Jan. 20, 2025 letter directed the dismissal of DHS advisory committee members.
The committees included advisory bodies covering emergency preparedness, telecommunications, science and technology, AI, and cybersecurity.
unsupported_original_claims: The source concerns Department of Homeland Security committees, not advisory boards connected to the Joint Chiefs of Staff or the Defense Department.
The source does not establish the removal of dozens of former generals or a degradation of military readiness advice.

corrected_claim.title: DHS Orders Dismissal of Its Advisory Committee Members
corrected_claim.claim: On Jan. 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman sent a letter directing the dismissal of members of DHS advisory committees. The reported action did not concern Joint Chiefs or Defense Department advisory boards.

access_notes: Reuters report directly opened; the correction retains the agency and action described by the source.
evidence_gap: A primary Defense Department or Joint Chiefs notice is needed to substantiate the separate board-purge event in the frozen original.

sources.title: Trump Administration: Follow the Law
sources.access_notes: White House release opened. It lists federal investigations and lawsuits involving sanctuary jurisdictions, including New York and Illinois/Chicago.

sources.title: Protecting the American People Against Invasion
sources.access_notes: Executive order linked in the packet; it sets immigration-enforcement priorities but does not document March threats against states for filing suit.

supported_facts: The administration publicly described DOJ actions and lawsuits involving sanctuary jurisdictions, including New York and Illinois/Chicago, in a February 2025 White House release.
The January 20 executive order directed federal immigration-enforcement priorities.
unsupported_original_claims: The sources do not show a March 2025 statement naming California, New York, and Illinois and threatening retaliation because their officials litigated against Trump policies.
They do not establish an explicit threat to withhold federal funding from those states for protected court challenges.

corrected_claim.title: White House Describes Federal Actions Against Sanctuary Jurisdictions
corrected_claim.claim: In February 2025, the White House listed federal actions and lawsuits involving sanctuary jurisdictions, including New York and Illinois/Chicago. The cited material does not show that Trump threatened the named states with funding retaliation for filing lawsuits.

access_notes: White House release directly opened; its listed enforcement actions are distinct from the original alleged March retaliation threats.
evidence_gap: The alleged March public statements naming California, New York, and Illinois require a direct transcript, post, or contemporaneous report; the cited sources do not establish them.

sources.title: Trump says Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack was horrible, Israel should wrap up war
sources.access_notes: Reuters report opened. It quotes Trump saying Israel should finish its war and describes him defending Israel’s response while warning of lost international support.

supported_facts: On March 25, 2024, Trump said Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack was among the saddest things he had seen and said Israel needed to finish its war.
He also said Israel was losing international support and should wrap up the war.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited statement occurred in March 2024, not on Oct. 8, 2023.
This source does not support the separate post-inauguration claims about UN ceasefire votes, weapons transfers, or a continuing administration posture.
“Unconditional support” and a call to “finish the job” do not accurately summarize this interview.

corrected_claim.title: Trump Says Israel Should Wrap Up Gaza War While Criticizing Hamas
corrected_claim.claim: In a March 25, 2024 interview, Trump described Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack as horrible, said Israel should finish the war, and warned that Israel was losing international support.

access_notes: Reuters report directly opened and read.
evidence_gap: The administration-era claims about Security Council votes, weapons transfers, aid conditions, and international-court accusations require separate dated sources and should not be combined with this 2024 interview.

sources.title: The Trump-Kim Jong Un timeline
sources.access_notes: Timeline opened. It dates the “fire and fury” threat to Aug. 8, 2017 and places “fell in love” in the 2018 relationship period.

sources.title: Press Conference by President Trump
sources.access_notes: Archived Singapore summit transcript linked in the packet; it documents the 2018 summit, not the 2017 threat.

supported_facts: Trump threatened North Korea with “fire and fury” on Aug. 8, 2017.
His “I fell in love” remark about Kim came in 2018 after the Singapore summit, not days or weeks before the 2017 threat.
unsupported_original_claims: The entry combines rhetoric separated by months and assigns the later “fell in love” remarks to the 2017 period.
The sources do not support a direct sequence of affectionate remarks followed days later by nuclear threats.
Claims about allied confusion and diplomatic incoherence are interpretations, not directly sourced facts in these records.

corrected_claim.title: Trump’s North Korea Rhetoric Shifted From 2017 Threats to 2018 Summit Praise
corrected_claim.claim: Trump threatened North Korea with “fire and fury” in August 2017; after the 2018 Singapore summit he later said he and Kim had “fallen in love.” The remarks belong to separate phases of their relationship.

access_notes: Washington Post timeline opened; archived White House summit transcript linked as primary context.
evidence_gap: The entry does not identify a single discrete incident in which the affectionate remark and nuclear threat were close in time; any separate use of “my friend” or “great leader” needs its own dated source.

sources.title: Report on the Investigation into Russian Interference in the 2016 Presidential Election, Volume II
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Special Counsel Robert S. Mueller III
sources.access_notes: Official Mueller report cited in the packet. Firecrawl returned a rate-limit error during this check; prior packet notes identify the report’s account of Trump directing the Air Force One statement.

supported_facts: The Mueller report describes Trump directing the creation of a public statement about Donald Trump Jr.’s June 2016 Trump Tower meeting while aboard Air Force One.
The statement described the meeting as concerning adoption; Mueller examined the episode as part of its obstruction analysis.
unsupported_original_claims: The report and supporting source record do not establish that John Dowd drafted the statement; the entry names him as the drafter without a verified attribution.
The claim that Dowd resigned partly over this statement is not supported by the cited report.

corrected_claim.title: Mueller Report Describes Trump Directing a Statement About Trump Tower Meeting
corrected_claim.claim: The Mueller report says Trump directed the drafting of a public statement aboard Air Force One describing Donald Trump Jr.’s 2016 Trump Tower meeting as concerning adoption. The cited report does not establish John Dowd as its drafter.

access_notes: The government PDF is the exact cited primary source, but the current verification attempt hit Firecrawl’s rate limit; the packet’s prior review had opened and summarized the relevant section.
evidence_gap: A page-level citation or contemporaneous account naming the actual drafter is needed before asserting that John Dowd wrote the statement.

sources.title: U.S. Senate confirms Trump’s nominee Pam Bondi as attorney general
sources.access_notes: Reuters article opened. It reports Bondi’s 54–46 Senate confirmation vote on Feb. 4, 2025.

sources.title: New Records Shed Light on Donald Trump’s $25,000 Gift to Florida Official
sources.access_notes: Article text returned in Exa’s search excerpt. It describes the 2013 donation and contemporaneous review of Trump University complaints by Bondi’s office.

supported_facts: The Senate confirmed Pam Bondi as attorney general on Feb. 4, 2025, by a 54–46 vote.
The Trump Foundation sent $25,000 to Bondi’s political fundraising committee in 2013; her office was reviewing Trump University complaints around that period.
unsupported_original_claims: Jan. 22, 2025 is not Bondi’s confirmation date.
The sources document a donation and timing, but do not establish a quid pro quo or a criminal finding.
The characterization of this as a proven “corruption record” is not a discrete fact established by the cited evidence.

corrected_claim.title: Senate Confirms Pam Bondi After Scrutiny of a 2013 Trump Foundation Donation
corrected_claim.claim: The Senate confirmed Pam Bondi as attorney general on Feb. 4, 2025. Earlier reporting documented a $25,000 Trump Foundation donation to her political committee in 2013 while her office was reviewing Trump University complaints; the donation does not by itself establish a quid pro quo.

access_notes: Reuters confirmation report opened; New York Times article text was available in a search excerpt. No source reviewed establishes an exchange or criminal quid pro quo.
evidence_gap: Primary campaign-finance filings and any contemporaneous investigation records would be needed to resolve the donation’s timing and decision process beyond the cited reporting.

sources.title: White House says Musk is not DOGE employee, has no authority to make decisions
sources.access_notes: Reuters report opened. It summarizes the White House’s court filing that Musk was a senior adviser, not a DOGE employee, and could advise the president but not make decisions.

sources.title: Judges to consider barring Musk’s DOGE team from government systems
sources.access_notes: Source linked by the current packet proposal for litigation over DOGE access to government systems.

supported_facts: The White House told a federal court that Musk was a senior adviser to the president rather than a DOGE employee and had no decision-making authority.
DOGE personnel’s access to government systems faced legal challenges.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited evidence does not establish that courts repeatedly ruled DOGE’s operations unconstitutional or that those rulings were ignored.
The claims that Musk personally accessed classified systems, shut agencies, or redirected contracts are not established by these two sources.
“No legal authorization” and “shadow executive branch” are legal conclusions broader than the cited court filing.

corrected_claim.title: White House Tells Court Musk Was an Adviser Without DOGE Decision Authority
corrected_claim.claim: In February 2025, the White House told a federal court that Elon Musk was a senior adviser, not a DOGE employee, and could advise the president but had no decision-making authority. DOGE access to government systems was separately challenged in court.

access_notes: Reuters court-filing report directly opened; the second cited link is Reuters coverage carried by Investing.com.
evidence_gap: Specific judicial holdings, their scope and enforcement, and claims about classified access or DOGE operational acts need case-specific court orders and records.
